title: “LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: Why Would God Put a Sentence Like This in Scripture?
paragraphs: “LET HER BREASTS SATISFY YOU”: Why Would God Put a Sentence Like This in Scripture?
We have spent generations whispering about something the Bible was never embarrassed to say out loud—and Proverbs 5:19 may expose far more than our discomfort with sex.
There are verses people frame and hang on walls.
There are verses printed on coffee mugs.
There are verses whispered beside hospital beds, preached at funerals, written inside wedding cards, and highlighted until the paper nearly tears.
And then there is Proverbs 5:19.
“Let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
Yes.
That is in the Bible.
Not in an ancient piece of erotic literature somebody accidentally slipped between Ecclesiastes and Isaiah.
Not in some modern paraphrase trying to make Scripture provocative.
It is Proverbs.
Wisdom literature.
Holy Scripture.
And perhaps the question is not, “Why would God allow something like that in His Word?”
Perhaps the more uncomfortable question is...
Why does it embarrass us more than it apparently embarrassed God?
Stay with me, because this verse is not permission for lust.
It is almost the exact opposite.

And if you have ever struggled with pornography, adultery, wandering eyes, sexual shame, a wounded marriage, secret fantasy, loneliness, temptation, or the feeling that Christianity treats human desire as something filthy, Proverbs 5 may be far more beautiful—and far more confronting—than you were ever told.
The Hebrew does not sanitize the verse.
It says:
אַיֶּלֶת אֲהָבִים וְיַעֲלַת־חֵן דַּדֶּיהָ יְרַוֻּךָ בְכָל־עֵת בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
Ayyélet ahavim veya'alat-chen, daddeha yeravvukha bekhol-et; be'ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The language is tender, poetic—and unmistakably physical.
The woman is pictured as a loving doe, a graceful deer. Her husband is told to find satisfaction in her breasts and to remain continually captivated, even intoxicated, by her love.
The Hebrew does not apologize.
But neither does it isolate her body from covenant love.
That is where our culture—and sometimes even Christians reading this verse too quickly—can completely miss the point.
Because Proverbs 5:19 did not fall out of heaven as a random sentence about breasts.
Read what comes immediately before it.
“Drink water from your own cistern, and running water out of thine own well.”
Then:
“Let thy fountain be blessed: and rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And immediately after the famous verse comes the question:
“And why wilt thou, my son, be ravished with a strange woman, and embrace the bosom of a stranger?”
Do you see it?
This is not God telling a man to objectify women.
This is a father warning his son not to destroy himself through sexual unfaithfulness.

The chapter begins with warnings concerning forbidden sexual relationships. It describes temptation as something that can initially seem sweet and attractive but eventually become bitter and destructive.
Then Scripture does something remarkable.
It does not merely say:
Don’t.
Don’t desire.
Don’t feel.
Don’t touch.
Don’t enjoy.
Instead, biblical wisdom redirects desire toward covenant.
Rejoice in your wife.
Delight in her.
Be captivated by her.
Remain intoxicated with her love.
In other words, God does not answer destructive desire merely by commanding the death of desire.
He teaches desire where to go.
That changes everything.
Because somewhere along the way many believers absorbed an idea the Bible itself never teaches:
That holiness means becoming almost embarrassed by the body.
Yet the first human body was not invented by pornography.
God invented it.
Sexuality was not created in a nightclub.
God created male and female.
Marriage was not invented by Hollywood.
God established covenant companionship before humanity's fall.
Sin did not create desire.
Sin distorts desire.
And there is an enormous difference.
Pornography takes something capable of covenant intimacy and removes covenant.
Lust takes a person and reduces that person to consumption.
Adultery takes desire outside the boundaries of faithfulness.
Sexual exploitation takes what should involve dignity and turns another human being into an instrument.
But Proverbs 5 paints another picture.
A husband.
A wife.
A covenant.
Exclusive affection.
Joy without betrayal.
Desire without theft.
Intimacy without strangers.
A body cherished within faithful love.
That is why verse 19 cannot honestly be separated from verse 18:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
And it cannot be separated from verse 20:
Why become captivated by another woman?
The entire contrast is between covenant faithfulness and covenant betrayal.
And then comes a sentence that should sober anyone living a secret sexual life:
“For the ways of man are before the eyes of the LORD.”
The browser history nobody knows about.
The conversation you keep deleting.
The emotional affair you keep renaming “friendship.”
The private messages.
The second account.
The fantasies you deliberately feed.
The person at work whose attention you have begun craving.
The marriage you have emotionally abandoned while continuing to occupy the same house.
God sees.
Not because He is some cosmic voyeur waiting eagerly to humiliate you.
He sees because nothing that is destroying you is invisible to Him.
And this is where Proverbs 5 becomes painfully personal.
Maybe the scandal is not that God mentions a woman's breasts.
Maybe the scandal is that we live in a culture drowning in sexual imagery while starving for covenant intimacy.
Bodies everywhere.
Faithfulness becoming rare.
Sex everywhere.
Tenderness disappearing.
Access everywhere.
Intimacy nowhere.
People learning thousands of ways to stimulate themselves while forgetting how to give themselves faithfully to another human being.
And pornography may be one of the clearest examples.
Porn promises intimacy without vulnerability.
Pleasure without covenant.
Bodies without responsibility.
Excitement without faithfulness.
It trains the eyes to consume while Proverbs trains the heart to cherish.
Porn says:
More.
Different.
Next.
Someone else.
Proverbs says:
Rejoice in the wife of your youth.
There is something profoundly countercultural about that.
Biblical sexuality is not built around endless novelty.
It is built around faithful rediscovery.
The same covenant.
The same person.
Years passing.
Bodies changing.
Hair graying.
Scars appearing.
Children coming—or perhaps never coming.
Illness.
Arguments.
Forgiveness.
Ordinary mornings.
Difficult seasons.
And somehow...
“Rejoice.”
That may be more radical than anything our hypersexual culture has imagined.
Because lust asks:
“What can I take?”
Covenant asks:
“How can I love?”
Lust consumes bodies.
Love knows names.
Lust hides.
Covenant remains.
Lust continually needs another image.
Faithful love learns to see the same person more deeply.
And maybe someone reading this already feels the shame rising.
Because you crossed the line.
Maybe years ago.
Maybe last night.
Maybe ten minutes before you found this article.
Perhaps your marriage is wounded because of what you did.
Perhaps nobody knows.
Perhaps everybody knows.
Maybe pornography has become the secret room you enter whenever loneliness becomes unbearable.
Maybe you promised God a hundred times:
“Never again.”
And then again happened.
And again.
And again.
Eventually you stopped making promises because breaking them hurt too much.
Listen carefully.
The Gospel is not pretending sin does not matter.
Jesus never needed to minimize sin in order to maximize grace.
The cross proves precisely how serious sin is.
But the cross also proves something else.
Your sin does not get the final sentence if you belong to Christ.
There is repentance.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a Savior who already knew the ugliest chapter before He called your name.
Christianity does not announce:
Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.
The Gospel announces that sinners can come to Christ, repent, believe, be forgiven, and begin becoming new.
That does not mean consequences magically disappear.
Trust may need rebuilding.
A wounded spouse may need time.
Secret patterns may need confession, accountability, pastoral care, counseling, boundaries, and radical changes in behavior.
Repentance is more than feeling terrible after sin.
Repentance turns around.
But shame says:
Hide.
Jesus says:
Come.
Shame says:
You are what you did.
Grace says:
Christ can make you new.
Shame says:
This chapter ruined the entire story.
Then Jesus walks into stories everybody else thought were finished.
That is the Gospel Warrior message.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Not because sin is cute.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
And perhaps that is why Proverbs 5:19 matters so much.
It reveals a God who is not embarrassed by faithful marital intimacy.
A God who created human beings as embodied creatures.
A God who condemns adultery while honoring covenant delight.
A God whose answer to sexual chaos is not shame but holiness.
Not repression, but rightly ordered love.
Not exploitation, but covenant.
Not secrecy, but truth.
Not endless consumption, but faithful delight.
And ultimately...
not merely behavior modification.
Christ.
Because you can install every filter and still have a heart that wants darkness.
You can throw away your phone and still carry lust inside you.
You can learn religious vocabulary while remaining inwardly enslaved.
We need more than restraint.
We need redemption.
We need new hearts.
We need the mercy of Jesus Christ.
Maybe this article found you while you are fighting something nobody knows about.
Then stop pretending with God.
He already knows.
Bring it into the light.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to confess, confess wisely.
If you need accountability, seek it.
If you have wounded your spouse, stop defending yourself and begin rebuilding truthfully.

If your marriage has become emotionally cold, do not use Proverbs 5:19 as a demand for sex. The verse is not a weapon for coercing a spouse. Biblical marital intimacy belongs inside love, honor, mutual care, faithfulness, and dignity.
Your spouse is not an entitlement.
Your spouse is a person to love.
And if you are unmarried, this passage is not telling you that you are incomplete.
Christ is not a consolation prize until marriage arrives.
The deepest identity of a Christian is not husband, wife, boyfriend, girlfriend, virgin, divorced, widowed, betrayed, or sexually broken.
It is found in Christ.
Maybe you have spent years believing your sexual past disqualified you from being deeply loved by God.
It does not.
Repentance does not rewrite history.
Jesus redeems sinners within history.
The scars may remain.
But scars are not always evidence that the story ended badly.
Sometimes scars prove the wound did not kill you.
Look at the risen Christ.
Even resurrection did not erase every scar.
And maybe somebody you know desperately needs to hear that.
Send this privately to the friend drowning in pornography.
Send it to the believer carrying sexual shame.
Send it to the marriage trying to rebuild after betrayal.
Because temptation has a strange ability to make us forget in the moment what we knew clearly yesterday.
If this exposed something hidden, you do not need to write the details publicly.

And if Christ has already brought you out of sexual bondage, shame, adultery, pornography, or a broken season, consider leaving a testimony—not to glorify the darkness you escaped, but to tell somebody still trapped inside it that chains really can break.
No performance.
No pretending.
Just truth.
And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, grow deeper in Christ, confront sin, understand grace, and walk more faithfully with Jesus, stay close.
But hear this clearly:
It does not replace obedience to Christ.
It does not buy blessing.
Scripture says Christian generosity should come from the heart, “not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
And sometimes supporting Gospel work is not only financial.
Leave thinking about faithfulness.
About what your eyes belong to.
About what your heart has been feeding.
About the person you promised to love.
About the secrets you need to bring into the light.
About the grace you thought you had exhausted.
About the Savior who still receives repentant sinners.
Because one day the secret tab closes.
The fantasy ends.
The body ages.
The applause disappears.
The temptation that once seemed irresistible becomes dust.
And what remains is the question beneath Proverbs 5 all along:
What kind of person are you becoming when nobody else is watching?
God is not embarrassed by holy desire.
He wants to rescue desire from everything that turns love into consumption and people into objects.
And perhaps tonight, the most intimate thing you can do is not touch another body.
Perhaps it is finally to stop hiding your soul.
Come into the light.
Come back to covenant.
Come back to truth.
Come back to Jesus.
Because the chapter you are most ashamed of may become the place where someone else finally discovers what grace actually means.
The sin that told you to hide may become the scar through which somebody else finally sees the light of Christ.
